title: The Law of the Righteous and the Vanity of Luxury
english: Our God and Savior does not instruct men by decisive and dogmatic decrees alone, so as to hate evil and love virtue, but He also provides clear lessons of the good life through vivid examples, advancing us through both deeds and words to the grasp of a good and God-loving life.

In this same way, even now, having warned us often through prophetic and evangelical mouths, and not only so but also through a familiar voice, to turn away from the proud and exalted wealth, and to love a philanthropic mind and a poverty lived with justice, so that the good counsel might be more firmly established, He proves the word with practical examples and writes through the narrative the rich man and the poor man (Luke 16:19-31).

He shows the one the enjoyment of ambition and the other the distressed life, and the end of both lives in that to which they arrived, so that, having considered the truth for the benefit of others, we might become prudent judges of our own.

A certain man was rich and was clothed in purple and fine linen. Through two concise names, the word examines and mocks the sprawling and immoderate dissipation of those who wealthily live badly. For the color of the purple is costly and elaborate, but the use of the fine linen is not necessary. For those choosing a prosperous life, it is simple, familiar, and friendly to measure the use of necessary things according to need, and to flee from the vain emptiness of the one dragged by and the many-layered diversion as the mother of evil.

And so that we may learn the power of this said thing more clearly, let the use of clothing be first recognized, to what extent and by what limits it will be received, encompassing prudence. What then...

The law of the righteous says: God created the sheep with an easy nature, whose wool grows straight. Taking this ready material, give to the weaver's art the substance, and fashion for yourself a tunic and a garment, so that you may escape the hardship of winter and the harm of the scorching ray.

If you also have need of lighter clothing during the season of summer, God gave the use of linen for a wider enjoyment; and it is easy for you to acquire from there a beautiful covering, simultaneously wearing and refreshing through its lightness. And enjoying these things, one confesses to the Creator the grace for which He provided not only us, but also the security for living.

But if, leaving behind the sheep and the wool and the necessary preparation of the Creator of all things, one, dividing the fine fabric through vain thoughts and reckless desires, seeks the fine fabric and gathers the threads of the Persian worms, weaving a spider-like web, and coming toward the flower-colored dye, pays a lavish wage, so that having hunted the murex from the sea, he may anoint the garment with the blood of the animal—this is a man exceeding in excess, being colored by his possessions, having no place to pour out the surplus. And because of this, it is reasonable that such a person is scourged by the Gospel, being accused as foolish and effeminate, being mocked by the worlds of brave maidens.

Others again are lovers of the same vanity; rather, having practiced more evil, they have not even set the limits of foolish thought at what has been said, but having discovered some empty and curious weaving, which imitates the power of the saffron garment in its chest-fold toward the crocus, and marks the forms of all animals with its veils, having loved the art of making garments for themselves, for women, and for children, being multicolored with flowers and myriad images; they are playing, not striving.
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: The Deception of Luxury
english: By misusing the immeasurable wealth of life, not using it, and acting lawlessly against Paul, they fight not with letters but with deeds. For he proclaimed with word what these hold and rule with works. When they appear clothed, they are seen like walls painted by passers-by. Even children stand around them, laughing at one another and pointing to the writing on the garments; and they walk past, not stopping for long.

There are lions and leopards, bears and bulls and dogs; woods and rocks, and men beast-slayers, and all the skill of painting imitating nature. For it was necessary not only their walls, as it seems, and their houses to be decorated, but already also their tunics and the clothes upon them.

As for those who are more pious than the wealthy ones, having reviewed the Gospel history, they handed it over to the weavers; I say the Christ our Lord meeting with the disciples, each miracle as the narrative has it: the wedding in Galilee and the water; the paralytic carrying the bed on his shoulders (Mark 2:1-12); the blind man being healed with mud (Matthew 8:1-4); the woman bleeding being taken by the edge of the garment (Luke 8:43); the sinful woman falling at the feet of Jesus (Luke 7:36-50); Lazarus returning to life from the tomb (John 11:1-44).

And doing these things, they think they are being pious and putting on garments graced by God. But if they accept counsel, let them, having sold those things, honor the living icons of God. Do not paint Christ; for it is enough for Him the one part of the incarnation, humility, which He freely received through us, but carry the incorporeal Word mentally upon your soul. Do not have the paralytic on your garments, but seek the one lying sick. Do not constantly recount the woman bleeding, but have mercy on the grieving widow. Do not look carefully at the sinful woman prostrating herself before the Lord, but let the tear flow thick, being crushed by his own faults. Do not sketch Lazarus being raised from the dead, but prepare a good defense for your own resurrection. Do not carry the blind man on your clothing, but the living one deprived of sight.

Encourage with acts of goodness. Do not paint the remains of the dead in a flattering way, but nourish those who hunger. Do not carry the water-skins upon the garments, which He filled in Cana of Galilee (John 2:7), but give drink to the thirsty.

Regarding these things, the proud clothing of the richman benefited us, and not only that, but also what follows. For luxury was added to the purple and the fine linen daily and brilliantly; yet, in both respects, it is of one single mind: to be adorned by useless vanity in delicacies, and to serve the palate and the throat with pleasant sensations.

Luxury, therefore, is a thing hostile to a virtuous life, signifying emptiness and dissipation, excessive enjoyment and a slave-like habit. And while the thing appears to be one, when examined in parts and accused, its composition consists of a diverse, greater, and manifold evil. For luxury could not exist unless increased by many materials. But as for accumulating the materials of wealth, one might without sin fail to lose nothing, unless, perhaps, according to the small measure, as with Job (Job 1:10), it should happen to one both to prosper abundantly and to live strictly according to justice.

Therefore, it is necessary for one living in luxury, first, to have a costly house, decorated with votes, stones, and gold according to the patterns, and to have it conveniently suited to the changes of the seasons of the year. For warmth is sought; the winter is wretched and turned away from the midday sun, having risen toward the North, while the summer is [warm], so that it may be breathed upon by thin and cold northern breezes. After this, there is the need for costly clothing for the beds, the couches, the mattresses, and the doors that are about to be clothed. For everything, even the inanimate things, is carefully clothed by those, as the wretched are stripped of their belongings.

Add to these also and consider the silver in the vessels, the gold, the expensive purchase of birds from Phasais, and the wine of the Phoenician, which the vines of Tyre pour out much and precious to the rich; and all the preparation of the rest of enjoyment, which those using it have carefully named. For luxury, increasing daily toward the more curious, already pours out the scents from India upon the faces, and more so, the perfumers serve the cooks rather than the physicians.

title: The Poverty and Misery of Lazarus
english: Consider the crowd of attendants at a banquet: the table-preparers, the wine-pourers, the stewards, and those who lead them, the musicians, dancers, flute-players, comedians, flatterers, and parasites, following the trail of vanity. To acquire these, how many poor are wronged! How many orphans are crushed! How many widows weep! How many, being violently torn apart, rush toward strangulation. The soul of such a person, having tasted some water of Lethe, completely forgets who she is and with whom she is joined, and that she will one day be released from this union and, having been resurrected, will dwell again with the body. But when the time of the necessary and appointed command comes, which severs her from the fellowship with the body, a calculation of what has been lived enters, and a useless repentance occurs after the need has arisen. For regret is only a sorrow when the one reconsidering still has the power to correct; but when the activity of the one doing right has been taken away, sorrow is worthless and the change of mind is vain.

There was once a man named Lazarus (Luke 16:20). The word does not describe him as a mere poor man, but as one deprived of the necessities of spending and need, and also being tormented by painful sickness and having a body broken, homeless, unsupported, untreated, thrown at the gate of the rich. And with great care in the narration, he brings the misfortunes of the poor to a tragic climax, so as to expose the hardness of the one who does not show mercy. For he who suffers nothing from hunger or disease is an irrational beast, pitiless or sympathetic, a form badly shaped into a human, falsely pretending nature by his intention; rather, he is even more unsympathetic than the beasts themselves; for even pigs, when one is being slaughtered, are drawn to a certain sad sensation and trouble the butcher with their blood; but oxen stand by such a slaughter, empathizing with a sound, signaling the pain. And herds of sheep, when one of the flock falls into the clutches of wild beasts, fall into a state where the one held is being sought, and some mournful sound fills the air, seeking its kind and companion. But a human, the rational animal, who is day-by-day being educated in goodness according to the likeness of God, cares so little...

Oh, the relatives in the painful circumstances of misfortunes! Thus lay the much-painful and blessed poor man, not having feet, for he would have fled the insolent and proud one, having changed to another place; instead of the murderous gate, being deprived of hands by the closed hands of the poor, and not even having a palm to stretch out for a request, being obstructed by those very organs of the voice and producing a certain hoarse and rough sound of the sternum, simply maimed in all his limbs, leaving behind a wicked disease, a pitiful example of human weakness.

But nevertheless, not even such a list of misfortunes turned the Exalted toward a visit; rather, He leaves the man like a stone, unresolving the sin being perfected. For he did not have the common and respectable things to say to accuse: 'I did not know, I did not realize; the poor man eluded me, my mistress.' He lay before the gate, a spectacle of entering and exiting, so that he might work out the necessary judgment of the proud one. He desired even the crumbs of the table and did not even obtain these; but one was bursting from abundance, and the other was melting from want.

It was indeed good and just for that Canaanite, that Phoenician woman, to teach the wealthy misanthrope, saying those things written: 'O insolent and proud one, and the dogs eat from the crumbs falling from the table of their masters (Luke 16:21); but you did not deserve this gift for your brother, your kindred?'

But the dogs were carefully fed, especially the watchdogs; and they were worthy of a roof and a bed and had attendants appointed with haste, but the image of God was thrown down, neglected and trampled, which the Master Artist and Creator fashioned with His own hand, if Moses is reliable to demonstrate the origin of men.

If, then, the account of Lazarus ended thus, and such was the nature of things, as to describe our life by the irregularity of this life, I would have left great voices babbling, through which the created ones pass similarly, thus unequally among their kindred. Since, however, the things remaining are beautiful for listening, in the...

title: The true meaning of poverty and the example of Lazarus
english: The poor man passes by sighing, having learned through his companions the blessed enjoyment of your fellow-sufferer. For you will find a precise judgment-court of the righteous Judge, in which the one who enjoyed pleasure sighs, and the one who lived in luxury is distressed; and each is carried to what is due to him.

And it happened that the poor man died and was carried by the angels into the bosom of Abraham (Luke 16:22). Do you see the ministers of the righteous and the poor, and the servants of the transfer? For angels were bearing him, looking at him calmly and gently, and by their appearance foretelling the healing and relief awaiting him. And he was placed, having been carried to the bosoms of the patriarch, which provides a starting point for the pleasureless to torture the depths of the Scriptures.

For if every dying person were carried to the same place, someone great would be an infinitely filling bosom, if it were to be capable of containing the multitude of the holy ones. But if this is utterly impossible, for a bosom, having been hollowed out, barely contains one man or with difficulty two, some divine vision receives us by the image of the sensible bosom, guiding us toward some intelligible reality.

For what is it that is being said? Abraham, it is said, receives those who have lived a prosperous life. Tell me then, O law-giver Luke, as if to one present and visible, I will discourse with you: why, being among many righteous ones and elders of Abraham, did you allot this honor to the drunkard, remaining silent about Enoch, Noah, and if anyone else who was not following these during his life? But perhaps I understand you, and what I consider does not cast you out from your purpose.

Since Abraham is a servant of Christ, and this man received the manifestations of Christ differently from men, and the mystery of the Trinity was sufficiently expressed to us in the tent of this old man, when he welcomed the three angels as traveling companions; and simply, from many mystical enigmas, this man has become a familiar man of God, having later clothed himself in flesh and having clearly spoken to men through this human veil, therefore his bosom is like a pleasant harbor and an unshakeable rest.

He says it is the portion of the righteous. For in Christ is the salvation and the hope and the expectation of the coming age of all of us, through him having sprung from the flesh of Abraham according to the human lineage. And it seems to me that the honor concerning the old man has a reference to the Savior, who is also judge and rewarder of virtue, and with the therapeutic voice calling the righteous and saying: 'Come, you who are blessed by my Father, inherit the kingdom prepared for you' (Matt 25:34).

And the poor man came to die. There is a double significance concerning the poor man: one declaring the need of the necessary things, the other the moderation and the humility of character. Therefore, let him who lacks the things of the material world and labors for silver, being clothed in the garment of pity, claim the praise of virtue, and let him not consider the lack to be sufficient for salvation. For he who labors by necessity is not praised, but he who moderates his will freely is marveled at. Since for those who are destitute, if they have a way of life that is uneducated or uncontrolled, necessity becomes a supply for many and wicked daring acts. And I myself, all the wall-scrapers and men who walk on toes, and moreover looters and thieves and even murderers, if they ever passed by an official judgment, I have seen them as poor, unknown, destitute, and unhospitable.

From this it is evident that the Scripture now blesses that poor man who bears the hardships with a philosophical soul, enduring bravely toward the circumstances of life and doing no evil deed, so that he might be granted the enjoyment of luxury in the flesh. Whom the Lord also describes more clearly in the first of the beatitudes, saying: 'Blessed are the poor in spirit' (Matt 5:3). Therefore, not every poor man is righteous, but he who is like Lazarus; nor is every rich man rejected, but he who lives with such a choice of will as he who was contemporary with Lazarus; and of this, those who are witnesses through the trial of life are evident. title: The Poverty of Judas and the Fate of the Rich
english: Was he more wretched than Judas Iscariot? And he gained nothing from his poverty toward salvation, but while dining with the eleven poor ones and with the philosophers, and even with the Lord himself, who through us became voluntarily poor, he was driven there by a bad intention toward the love of money, and from there he contrived the betrayal.

It is also worthy to test the departure of another of the dead. For the poor man, having fallen asleep, had angels as guards and attendants, leading him with good hope to the place of rest; but the rich man, having died, is said to have been buried (Luke 16:22). For there is nothing like using that scriptural word, which through a single word sufficiently interprets the dishonorable dissolution of the rich.

For the sinner finishing his life is truly being buried, the body being earthly and of the soil, and the soul, having drawn the natural worth of that toward the sympathy of the flesh for matter, leaving behind no useful memorial of his own life, and being covered shamefully and finishing the death of the pastures. For the body has a tomb, but the soul has Hades; two dark prisons being divided for the punishment of the evil creature.
And who would not reproach the wretched one for his thoughtlessness? Whenever he was upon the earth, boasting, acting great, thinking himself above all the living and of the same nature and...

title: The Folly of the Flesh-Lovers
english: Only once does he call those who encounter him ants and worms, being torn apart by the empty wisdom of short-lived glory; but when he is snatched away from life and, like a slave of lashes, is deprived of those things of which through ignorance he thought himself a master, humility is brought upon him as a counter-response to pride. Like a goat putting forward the wails of a mourning woman, he calls upon the patriarch from afar and ignorantly, saying: 'Father Abraham, have mercy on me and send Lazarus, so that he may dip the tip of his finger in water and cool my tongue, for I am suffering in this flame' (Luke 16:24), seeking a mercy which was not given when it was easy for him to do good because he possessed the authority; and demanding that Lazarus arrive to help against the fire, praying to suck the finger of the leper slightly moistened with water. Such are the follies of the flesh-lovers; this is the end of the lovers of wealth and the lovers of pleasure.

And it is fitting for the prudent and the provident of the future, having taken as a parable something like a preventative medicine for a disease, to flee the experience of such evils, regarding compassion and philanthropy as the cause of life.

title: The Severity of Divine Judgment
english: Regarding the discipline that is to come, having practiced it. For the word has dramatically set out the admonition upon specific persons, so that, having been taught the law of the good citizenship with life and demonstration, we might never despise the commands of the Scripture, fearing them only as far as a word, and not indeed leading the threat toward punishment.

For I know how many of men, being enticed by such insinuations, grant themselves the power to sin unhindered. But on the contrary, we are taught by the present Scripture that no forgiveness lightens the penalty of that judgment, nor does philanthropy diminish the appointed punishment, if it is necessary for the voices of the patriarch to confirm the word.

For having heard many supplications from the rich and a myriad of pitying voices, he was neither moved by the wailings nor did the pain depart from the one bitterly flogged, but with strict wisdom he ratified the righteous judgment, saying that God has allotted to each according to his worth; and to you, since you have lived in luxury according to the others...

title: The Chasm and the Separation of Good and Evil
english: The justice of the trespass has been imposed upon you through three afflictions; but to the one there, having been toiled and trodden down and being vexed by the bitterness of the fleshly life, a certain sweet and rejoicing state has been distributed here.

Moreover, he says there is a great chasm, which prevents them from intermingling with one another, and it separates those punishing from those being punished, so that both may clearly distinguish themselves from one another, having an unmixed enjoyment of the good and the evil. I think the sensory parable is an enigma of an intellectual theory. For let us not truly suppose a ditch actually dug there among the angels, like the trenches that happen in military camps, but Luke describes to us the separation of those who are divided from one another, both those according to virtue and those who lived otherwise, setting forth the image of the chasm (Luke 16:26).

And Isaiah, saying something like this, seals our mind: Is not the hand of the Lord too weak to save, or has his ear become heavy so as not to hear? (Isaiah 59:1). But your sins divide you from one another and from God.
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: The Steward as Sojourner
english: The same homily from the Gospel according to Luke concerning the steward of unrighteousness.

Many times I have said to you, while conversing, that a certain molded and false notion falling upon men multiplies sins and diminishes good things, which each of us ought to practice according to our own way of life. And this is to think that all things which we have in the use of life we have acquired as masters and lords. And because of this assumption, we contend fiercely on their behalf, and we fight, and we judge, and we are consumed to the extreme as if we were owners of possessions.

But the truth is not so, but rather strongly contrary. For all things of which we have received, they are not ours; nor indeed are we as owners and lords of this life, as if we were settled in our own house, but we are led as resident aliens and sojourners and migrants to where we do not want and when we do not expect. And we are deprived of the things that exist, when it seems good to the Lord, of the possession.

Therefore also the life of this wicked one is a changeable thing; and he who is glorious today is tomorrow wretched, worthy of pity and lamentation and help; he who is now prosperous and well-provided with the materials of wealth, a poor man after a little while, not even having the bread from his own house which is brought to life. And in this especially our God excels the dead, by being always the same and likewise to have and to have acquired life and glory and power without being taken away.

Wherefore then, how I came to this beginning of the word, it perhaps is already known to those having understanding and to lovers of learning. Luke, having reshaped a parable for us, clearly presented, in which he describes the steward of others' things being squeezed and distressed, because, as one who is cut and costly, he heard from the master of the goods and possessions: 'Give an account of your management and depart; for I will not allow you to occupy myself with mine as if they were your own.' This, however, is not an explanation of a thing having happened, but a shaping...

A rebuke to those covered by the words, training moral virtue. Therefore, let each man know that he is a manager of someone else's property, and having cast from his soul the pride of authority, let him take up the humble and reverent role of the one responsible and the steward, always awaiting his lord and with trembling writing his account.

For he is a resident alien, having received permission for a short use and a temporary stay. But if you doubt the well-known things, learn from what happens and be instructed by the unerring teacher, experience.

Whether you have acquired a field, having received it from your fathers or having become master through association with someone. Calculate then in your memory and count, if you are able, all those who possessed it before you; and impose upon the future time the mind to consider how many will rule over it after you. Tell me, then, whose lordship is distinct and exceptional: those who possessed it, those who have it, or those who are going to have it? For if anyone were to gather everyone by a mechanism, those who have possessed it would be found more numerous than the oxen.

Rather, if you truly wish to see what our life is like, remember once when traveling in summer, I saw a spreading tree, extending greatly in width and length, sufficient to fill the need of a house with its shade. Having been delighted by this, you went under it and, as far as it was possible, remained there.

And since it was necessary again to depart, while you were deliberating your arrival, another traveler appeared. You indeed had your baggage, the cloak, but he was cleaning his own and receiving all your things in a collection: the straw, the fire, the shade of the tree, the running water. And he had the reclining, while you had the walking; he was delighted there also, then he left; and the one tree in a single day became by chance a short-term lodging for ten strangers; and all that happened was for the one who is truly the Lord. So also are the possessions of the life spent here.
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: The Governance of the Senses
english: Many things please and nourish, but lordship belongs only to God, who possesses life incorruptibly and imperishably. I saw an inn, where a traveler stayed; he took many things from there without owning any: a bed, a table, vessels, a plate, and other various utensils. No one has ever used them for self-sufficiency, but rather someone comes, becomes greedy, acts impetuously, plunders the inn, and seeks what belongs to others as if it were his own.

Such is our life, brothers, and if anything of what has been said is more temporary. I marvel at those who say, 'my place' or 'my house,' so that they in vain claim ownership of what does not belong to them, and they embrace foreign things with three deceptive elements. Just as the masks of those performing wonders belong to no one in particular, but all the actors in the plays wear them, so others clothe themselves with the earth and its materials from others as if they were garments.

Tell me, is there anything more powerful than a kingdom? Yet search the kingdoms; seek royal robes, and you will find them sufficient, though they have clothed many kings. Likewise, the crowns, the purple robes, and the belts—all are an unstable inheritance, a common use passing from those traveling to those staying.

What of the value of the possessor—the tent, the silver chariot, the golden reed? The possessor does not always have these, nor always the same, except for a short time for each. Just as the bed of the journey receives different bodies at different times, so the symbols of rulers change for those using them.

From this, the apostle cried out many instructive voices regarding this mindset: he presents the form of this world, namely, 'as having nothing and possessing all' (1 Tim 6:7), and 'those using as if not using' (1 Cor 7:31). For all these tend toward one aim: that it was fitting for us to live as sojourners, remembering the covenant of the exodus.

And so that you may learn accurately that you are subject to laws and masterly canons, according to which it is fitting for you to live accurately, first understand from yourself that both your body and your soul are subject everywhere to the commands of virtue, and you are not even master of yourself; rather, it is fitting for you to manage both word and deed and all...

The movement of your life. You received a body from the Creator, composed of many parts and being managed by five senses for the needs of life. But even these are not free and autonomous, but each is a slave to laws.

And first, the eye hears; look at nature and behold what is beautiful to see: the sun, lighting the whole inhabited world; the moon, illuminating the dark and gloomy night; the other stars, which are not many, nor sufficient for us, providing the light from themselves, except for the beauty they reflect. Behold the earth, adorned with all kinds of plants and herbs; the sea lying flat like a level plain, when it is in a pure calm. To these and such things you have been accustomed to seeing; but the other sights, as many as introduce harm to the soul through sight, flee from them and run away, and impose a covering upon yourself so that you may not see. For it is better to darken the sense when it holds the cause of the works of darkness. For this reason, the Lord said to us yesterday through Matthew: 'Every man who looks at a woman to lust after her has already committed adultery with her in his heart' (Matthew 5:28); and it is better to cut it off when it looks disordered and with injury.

Hearing also has prohibitive commands against bad listening. For it is necessary that when it hears of certain good things, it should be uplifted and send the sense to the soul through the beneficial words. But if a companion of wickedness, a plague and a corruption, approaches it, it must repel the filth of sin like a venomous beast.

Let the tongue also be temperate with the mouth; let it speak the righteous things; and let it abstain from the forbidden: reviling, slandering, unjust accusation, backbiting against brothers, and blasphemy against God. But let it utter whatever is well-spoken, whatever is pious, whatever has the counsel of good deeds; and let every man say the things of the Psalmist: 'I said: I will guard my ways, lest I sin with my tongue' (Psalm 119:11); and that, 'Their tongues were a stumbling block' (Psalm 57:4); and that, 'What boasts a strong man in wickedness, the power of lawlessness?' (Psalm 73:4). All the day your tongue reckoned injustice; you made a snare like a sharpened razor.
Let the taste be of those things which benefit the stomach. Let the nose also be temperate, not always smelling luxury, nor the vapors of expensive myrrh.
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: The Folly of Waste and the Stewardship of Death
english: lifting up the fragrance to the head. For of such things even Isaiah is a severe accuser. Let the hand of the commandments also be remembered, so that it may not touch all things without restraint. Let it stretch out toward almsgiving, not toward plunder; let it keep its own, not gather the things of others; let it touch the weak and injured bodies through good visitation, not those trembling and occupied with fornication.

The word showed us how we are not masters of ourselves, but stewards. For everything subject to laws and commands is a slave and obedient to the Lawgiver. If even the members of our body are not free by their own power, but are regulated toward activities by a masterly will, what would anyone say regarding those who claim to have unrestrained ownership of gold and silver and earth and other things?

Nothing, man. You are a slave and all that is yours belongs to the Lord. For a slave does not have free property. For you were made naked unto this light; you received what you have according to the law of your Lord; either inheriting from a father, since thus God ordained—for parents, he says, divide things among children like dogs—or having acquired prosperity from marriage, and marriage and that which is upon it are ordained by God, or from commerce and agriculture and other opportunities, God having worked through them.

Behold then, it was shown that you received things that are not yours. Let us see then what else has been commanded to you and what kind of management is required over those things. Give to the hungry, clothe the naked, heal the injured, do not leave behind the destitute, the one cast out in the crossroads. Do not worry about yourself, nor care how you will live in the future. Even if you work these things, he says, you shall be honored by the Lawgiver; but if you disobey the commandment, you shall be punished bitterly.

I do not see these things as belonging to one who is self-willed or one living with absolute authority, but on the contrary, many and continuous commands show me a man reigning strongly and requiring accountability through masterly laws and the established constitution as a duty.

As for us, how we, having life as something irrational, look around at the wretched and the laboring being finished by misfortunes, yet we spend money willingly on vanities, feeding a multitude of the useless...

And they are drawn to the company of evil spirits; and again they scatter wealth on beast-fights and wild beasts, showing no pity even toward those in the hippodromes; and again they spend their prosperity on wonder-workers and imitators and the following destructive things!

We suffer a thing that is empty and near to madness. For where the expenditure brings in immeasurable profit and immortal salvation, we hold the silver very tightly, as if we would not let even a few obols fall from the hand; but where the loss becomes the sin of sinners and the cause of myriads of punishments and of that very punishment through fire, we flow out by our own command. And ambition anticipates the request; and having opened all doors, we let the wealth go out to those outside. This mindset is not that of slaves waiting for the master, but of profligate, drunken, and dissolute youths.

If you wish, listener, to see the fear of a steward managing what was entrusted with sober piety, unfold the book of David; seek those words where the man of many deeds says to God concerning his own end: 'O Lord, make known to me my end, and who is the number of my days, so that I may know what I am lacking' (Psalm 39:4). See how the disposition of the one who has made a vow is viewed through the word as if in an image: that he is bound, and he foresees the future and awaits the judgment, and he examines the appointed time, so that the unexpected arrangement might not seize him at the moment of departure; and having calculated, he seeks to see what the deficiency of his sojourn is, so that having hurried, he might make up for it before the one leading out comes.

For truly, the end of each of us is an image of a steward, if we were to compare one another's individual matters: what the dying man suffers, and what the one being cast out of the stewardship endures. Likewise, the one who is finishing also hands over the administration to others, just as a steward hands over the keys; that one is cast out of a field, this one of the whole world as if of a single village. The steward withdraws, having suffered for his own labors, such as vineyards, gardens, and houses; so what do you think the one who is finishing suffers? Does he not grieve for his possessions? Does he not look with pity upon his substance, as he is being torn away from it without choice, far from treasures?
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: The Stewardship of the Soul
english: Will they be treasuries? And when he arrives at the allotted place, hearing, 'Render the account of your stewardship; show how you heard the commandments, how you dealt with fellow-slaves, either kindly and philanthropically or, on the contrary, greedily and tyrannically, striking, beating, and depriving them of the grain-measure of alms.'

If he is able to make the master appeased by proving himself a good servant, it would be well for him; but if on the contrary, there are no longer whips and rods there, nor dark mills and iron pedals, but unquenchable fire and eternal darkness never illuminated by light, and the gnashing of teeth, which the gospel has clearly revealed to us (Matt 25:30).

Therefore, if he never casts out from here as if they were strangers, let him waste the world and let pleasure remain unhindered according to every sense. But if these things will be accomplished, even if we do not enjoy them for long, let us fear, brothers, the transfer from this place, and let us live in the time of sojourning as the Lord commanded; let us not be carried away as debtors, but let us walk free, being led by a good conscience, carrying the books of the life's citizenship unsearchably.

That rich man was a bad steward of this life, whose land was fruitful, because regarding the abundance of fruits, man did not counsel anything good, but opening the desire of the stomach and the wide and insatiable bellies of greed, he allotted everything to his own enjoyment, saying, 'I will pull down my barns and build greater, and I will say to my soul: You have many good things laid up, rest, eat, drink, rejoice' (Luke 12:19-20). And while he was speaking, the one taking him arrived. A terrible fellow-slave came to snatch him away from the stewardship; and what is the profit of a love-of-money plan?

And these things were written vividly for our instruction. But what is the experience of life? Not every single day do these things cry out through works; I showed us the one healthy in the middle of the day becoming dead before the onset of evening; and the one strengthening himself in the evening, not grasping the morning ray; and another perishing in the midst of eating and living. Who then is so foolish, as not to realize that every day another [comes] of this [place]...

Are we being moved from our stewardship? But the good and faithful steward, having trusted in his own management, has a will such as Paul had. For he, when the Lord was not hurrying, hastened to him and desired the dismissal and was willing to relinquish the stewardship, saying in one way: 'Wretched am I a man, who will rescue me from this body of death?' (Rom 7:24) and again: 'For to me it is good to be dissolved and to be with Christ' (Phil 1:23). But the earthly man, whose mindset is truly kin to the oxen, laments such things helplessly at the transition, like this man in the parable: 'What shall I do, since my lord is taking the stewardship from me? I am not able to dig, and I am ashamed to beg' (Luke 12:48).

His grief is that of the idle and the lover of pleasure. For to wail at the departure is a reproach of having been added to the estate and of lamenting the passionate enjoyments of the flesh, while the inability toward the work of an idle life and a fallen state is an accusation. For if he had had a habit of love for labor, he would not have feared digging.

If we take the parable allegorically toward the spiritual, after this transition, there is neither working nor having time for increase. And because of this, let no one say: 'I am not able to dig.' For even if he is able, no one forgives. This life holds the agriculture of the commandments, while the one coming holds the enjoyment. So if you worked nothing here, the vines remained, and you care excessively about the spade; nor will you benefit yourself by having time.

And of this, a clear pattern is given to us by the foolish virgins; who, being in want of oil, shamelessly asked of the wise, but they gained nothing, but turned away uselessly; the Word showing that no one has used a different oil in the presence of the bridegroom, that is, a different [oil] to achieve for oneself private enjoyment. For each has wrapped his own conduct like a garment, whether bright and precious or cheap and resembling the rags of a pauper. And it is not possible to strip it off, nor to exchange it and change to another, nor to be beautified and adorned from a loan or use at the time of judgment. But each remains as he is in the truth, whether...
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: The Purpose of Festivities and the Call to Virtue
english: Whether poor or rich. And these things are only to this extent.

What could we say regarding the forgiveness of debts [Luke 7:41], which the steward of injustice used as a consolation for himself among the evil ones, negotiating with his fellow slaves? For it is not easy to transform the written word into a consistent allegory. But what appeared to me after much observation is this: All people, as many as we negotiate with regarding the remission that is coming to us, by giving or forgiving what is foreign, we find ourselves acquiring profit. But I say 'foreign' refers to the things of the Master. For nothing is our own, but all are the possessions of His lordship.

Therefore, whenever anyone, sensing the end and the transfer from this place, lightens the burden of sins through small acts of kindness, or by forgiving debts to debtors or providing prosperity to the needy, giving the things of the Master, he acquires many friends who are to bear witness to his goodness before the Judge, and through their testimony, he prepares a welcome for his arrival. For those who have suffered well are said to bear witness before the Judge, not with voices as if teaching those who are ignorant, but as those who exclude the sinners from the punishment of the deed done against them. In the same way as the blood of Abel was said to cry out to God [Genesis 4:10], so also the good work shall be said to bear witness to the one who has done well in Christ Jesus our Lord; to whom be the glory through the ages of ages. Amen.

Regarding the same [man] according to greed: Christian men and men who are partakers of a heavenly calling; you, the separated people, and all who have come out of the cities to sit together for the present harmonious feast; for I encompass you all in a general proclamation. Did each of you, having set his mind upon it, realize and understand for whose sake we have been gathered? Instead of being honored as witnesses by the magnificent decorations of houses and by these annual assemblies, and for what purpose we look...
Having seen these things, our fathers established a rule; and did they leave the law strong for those who follow? (3.1.2)

Or was this expressed to us with a little more density in the mind, so that through our zeal for piety, these festivities are gathered as a common instruction for souls, so that honoring the witnesses, we might imitate the endurance of the martyrs for piety; so that, placing the ear of those gathered as students, we might learn something useful, which we did not know before, whether the security of a dogma, or the solution of a perplexing Scripture, or some word restoring the state of morals? (3.1.2)

But you seem to me to be abandoning the care of virtue and fleeing from the diligence concerning the soul, to turn all your concern toward the service of Mammon and the busyness of worldly affairs; some mingling with others, and some having run off to foreign things, and some recording those striving at the marketplaces, so that they might slander one another. (3.1.3)

But redirect your desire toward the Church; leave behind the love of silver, the marketplace, and the frenzied woman. Turn away from her as an unseemly companion who has attached herself to the crowd, beautifying herself with foreign materials and the flowers of the apothecary. Love this divine and soberly-sently ordered one, who looks on with dignity and without distraction. (3.1.4)

For thus Solomon says in the book of Proverbs: Do not abandon her, and she will endure for you. Love her and she will keep you. Do not pass by her in contempt, nor consider the things set before us at this table to be worthless, because it is possible for you to acquire possessions easily; but rather desire more, for we do not sit as shopkeepers carrying a yoke or a basket, but we seek one profit: the salvation of the disciple. (3.1.5)
There was read to us from the Acts of Paul a word to Festus and Agrippa, from Paul, the faithful apostle and wise orator. You have certainly seen, O listener, if... (3.2.1)
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: The Consequences of Greed
english: You have applied the mind so that it does not surrender the truth out of cowardice, but by winning the difficult criterion through bold speech in the healing of Agrippa, it softens it toward goodness, like beasts watching the handling of the Word.

3.2.2 Zechariah has prophesied and even now opens the door to us of the great mysteries of the Only-Begotten through the stone, having the sevenfold vision, by means of the golden lampstand, upon which are the seven lamps and the two olive branches (cf. Zech 4). Many of the following Scriptures possess a rich treasure of benefit, to all of which I wished to come and show you the straightness of the spiritual festival.

3.2.3 The promise of the former work hastens me toward the construction of this debt. For having begun to be overwhelmed by many accusations of greed, lest we failed to strip vanity of it, we have set the refutation of the accusation toward the present day. Listen therefore and become discerning judges of the truth, since you judge not by other things, but by your own salvation, and you carry all the condemning votes upon the responsible party, each having driven his own soul away like a house or a city.

3.3.1 Greed, therefore, is not only to covet silver along with other possessions and to desire to join to what is present that which does not belong, but, to speak more generally, to desire to have more in every matter than what is owed and what is required.

3.3.2 And indeed this overflow first suffered the devil, being an archangel and having been appointed over the most excellent life and order, yet conceiving tyranny and rebellion against the Divinity, the fool; then, having been cast down, having fallen into this surrounding air, he became an evil neighbor to our life.

3.3.3 For he did not grasp that which he pursued, the Divinity; and he lost that which he possessed, the archangelhood; an unfaithful slave who, through small acts of audacity, turned into a robber; a dog deprived of the myth and the meat among the Greeks, and having snatched not even the shadow, for how could he grasp an ungraspable thing?

3.3.4 After this, the first man, being enticed by pleasure, lost immortality through forbidden food, just as Esau later lost the firstborn things because of lentil stew (Gen 25:34). And these dialects and the many of the...

A love for more has introduced the voices of men into life. For those having overstepped with human arrogance, expecting to make heaven a path for themselves and making a ridiculous tower upon that vain ascent, they made the same-minded men into foreign-tongued men; and seeking the more which they had, they themselves were continued in this and left the human race to suffer in the hearing of senseless voices and the seeking of interpretations.

What then of Pharaoh? From where did he fall into diverse and varied scourges? Was it not because of greed and the desire to be lord over a foreign people and to not allow anything belonging to that kingdom from anywhere? And because of this, not having released the strangers, he destroyed his own: some in the plague of the firstborn, others in the pursuit by the sea. For I allow rivers to flow into blood, and an immeasurable generation of frogs, and filth of lice, and an outbreak of flies, and the death of the four-footed, and all the evils, by which Egypt was judged because of the greed of the ruler.

But elsewhere again we learned the end of sin: an incurable leprosy poured out upon the greedy one. Remind me also, if anyone is a lover of stories and a friend to the righteous Elisha, how the Syrian Naaman was cleansed of leprosy after washing in the Jordan, but how the disease passed to the child Gehazi, a greedy and unphilosophical youth, having sold the spiritual gift and the free healing of the teacher.

How then did Absalom become a rebel, the son of the gentle father, a flaming and impudent youth? Was it not by seeking the inheritance of the kingdom before the time, leaping upon others as a robber? And Judas, why did he cast out the remnant of the disciples, and instead of an apostle, he made himself a traitor? Was it not first acting as a thief in the treasury, and then the acquisition of dishonorable glory? Why do the Acts lament Ananias and Sapphira among the apostles? Was it not because they became thieves of their own and sacrilegious of the household's devoted things?

Perhaps even today the day will leave off counting the servants of greed. Leaving the old history, let us examine the experience following in life; for greed knows a beast, and whatever it takes, it is always at its peak and not...
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: The Greed of the Sick and the Weather-Watchers
english: Wasting away, joining with those who are sinking and going to an end. 3.4.1 Lust, the lover of bodies, even if it rages through desires for a long time, or even having reached priestly age itself or having grown old having seen what is desired and having cast off its bloom, finds a standing place for the disease. The stomach's lust withdraws, either having filled the belly or having become weak from digestive particles and having ceased the heightened appetite. The glory-seeker destroys himself with many flattering appearances of vanity. 3.4.2 And the disease of greed is an evil that is inseparable; and just like this ivy, the lush plant and evergreen, it climbs strongly and entwines itself around the trees upon which it intends to cling, and it does not withdraw, neither having suffered nor having dried up, unless someone cuts its coils with iron like a dragon; in this way, it is not easy to free the soul from such a thing, whether the body is being refreshed or having diminished, unless a sober thought comes and like a knife cuts the disease. 3.5.1 To those at home, the greedy man is unpleasant, to servants heavy, to friends useless, to strangers difficult to deal with, to neighbors a nuisance, to a cohabiting wife a burden, to children stingy and a meager provider, a bad overseer of himself, caring only by night, becoming thick during the day, reasoning with himself according to those who have strayed or are deviating; he is always complaining and groaning as if in need, not enjoying those present and seeking those absent, not using what is his own, but coveting what belongs to others. 3.5.2 The flock of such a man is a great burden, narrowing the enclosures upon which it is penned, covering the pastures in which it grazes; even if a fleshy sheep appears to be approaching, having left his own flock, he approaches with desire toward the one and the other. The same happens with the oxen, similarly with the horses, and no differently with the earth. Everything narrows the house and nothing is useful in use; for the insatiable one is not even enjoyable, but his house is near a tomb. For behold, even tombs are often filled with silver and gold, but the inhabitants do not possess them. The body is not nourished, no profit is found for the soul; for almsgiving does not prosper from the right hand.

What is the end of toil? Let someone warned by such a disease teach this. I know many, having learned through experience, that even in sickness they love money more than health; if a doctor suggests a way of treatment through some substance, such as celery, thyme, or anise, of which supply is inexhaustible, they obey the advice readily; but if some medicine is required that is varied and complex, and they are commanded to go to the druggist or the perfumer, they are more ready to let go of their soul or to loosen their purse. For being earthly, they consider the prudence of possessing earthly goods to be life itself.

These are greatly distressed by common good fortunes, but circumstances bring them joy. They pray that tax-free decrees may come so that they may increase their silver through interest; they desire to see those distressed by lenders, so that they may acquire the field or the vessel or the animal being cast off easily out of necessity. And they constantly look up toward the sky after the philosophers, those attentive to the things in the air, not seeking a command from a star, nor peering to see if any house belongs to one of the planets, but rather attending to the busy state of the air, if the appearing signs promise a flow of rain or hail. Even if they see something difficult approaching for the many, they rejoice in the misfortune of others.

They gather everything into storerooms, marking it securely and fastening it with two locks; they count haphazardly while measuring. And when the greedy one is occupied with such a hope, and finally dreams of becoming rich in the shadow-sketch of ideas, if a deep cloud occurs, he fears it as being dangerous. If light sprinkles the earth, he begins to tear up; but if even rain occurs sufficient to end the hail, it is a matter of complete mourning.

He therefore wanders about, scrutinizing everything regarding the grain as if a son were in danger, asking what shall heal, what machine is needed, so that for a long time it may suffice for many, so that it may escape the blight of the crops. Even if he feels a heat, as doctors have spread him out to differentiate it, he divides and cools himself, settling his toil, a shelter according to the midday.
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: The Perils of Inheritance and the Example of Lazarus
english: He acts like a wise man, stripping away the shadows of night, so that he may be lulled by the night breezes. Poverty stands by this man while he is toiling, seeking from the endangered grain and not giving; or if he does give, he gives grudgingly, and is himself barely covered by a half-measure of grain. Therefore, I urge you, such a person, not to engage in endless toil and hardship.

For both the luxurious covetous man, who limits his life to the stomach and other pleasures, thinking this to be the end of humanity, is worthy of pity. But the small-minded and short-spoken man has no measure of his wretchedness, taking the portion of many and not giving to himself, bringing his haste to nothing.

For who does not know that nothing of the things happening, except virtues, happens by itself, but we do something else in order that we may achieve something else? No one sails more by the act of sailing itself, nor does a farmer live by his labors for the sake of farming alone; but it is evident that both proceed with painful endurance, one to reap the fruitfulness of the earth, the other to carry off the wealth of maritime commerce. And you, say what your end is. Is it to gather things together? And what kind of end is this, to see having heaped up useless matter?

He says, 'The sight even delights me.' Has your own sickness not changed? For it is possible to soothe desire even with the money of others. If the glitter of silver delights you, sitting before the silversmiths, looking at the dense and shining light, or taking pleasure in various vessels, both those that carry food and those that pour; for the sight is easy and unhindered for you.

See also the silver-experts at the tables, constantly feeling and counting the coins; rather, having been persuaded, I will advise you: change your mind through something good. For correction is easy, since greed is not a necessity of nature, but an impulse of choice, which is not difficult to change for those choosing what is profitable.

Peer with your thought into the time hereafter, when you will not be, when a little earth will lie over you, your body folded up and senseless; and a few flakes of ash will cover the remains. Where then will the wealth and the gathered treasures be? Who will be the heir of those left behind? For not all...

That person will be the successor you expect. If you leave children, they might happen to stumble, and a greedy person like you might drive them away from the father's house while they are mourning. Even if you are poor and send the inheritance to some friends, do not treat the will as an unshakeable law, as an irrefutable and strong thing. A little haste makes the writing void. Do you not see those constantly struggling in the courts against wills, where lawyers lead various schemes, bringing in legal experts to strike against them, bringing in terrible rhetoricians as helpers, nurturing false witnesses, and corrupting the courts?

For this reason, regarding those things you see happening, instruct those who come after you. If you have wealth justly, use it properly, like the blessed Job; if unjustly, distribute it to those who were plundered, like a prisoner of war; or take what you received along with an addition, like Zacchaeus. If you do not have it, do not acquire it wickedly. For sin will follow you as a bitter provision on a necessary journey, and the enjoyment of what was acquired will be left to those you do not know. Then you will marvel at David saying, 'He stores up, but does not know to whom he will gather it' (Ps 69:8). And you will know the rich man, the opposite of Lazarus, who has been fully read to us from the Gospels, not composed as a myth for astonishment, but handed down as an exact type of what is to come.

The deep has been spread out, the kingdom has passed to another, the luxuries have been abolished; sin from those things has emigrated along with them like a shadow remaining to a walking body. And because of this, after the luxury of banquets and the elegant table, a thin drop of water is sought, departing from a finger thin from disease; and he calls the poor man the healer of punishment, who perhaps does not even have hands when he rushes to the gate; for he would have driven away the dogs that were licking the wounds. And he desires to mingle with Lazarus, who is seen from afar, but is divided by the trench or the chasm; not a pit truly dug or a trench made, as one sees the battle line of war on the plains, but the obstacle, I think, of the...
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: Greed as the Root of Evil
english: The word demonstrates the sins, which to the one known for his approach toward the righteous, held him back. And for me, the interpretation of the prophet Isaiah is sealed regarding a foolish people, heavily reproving and saying: 'Is not the hand of the Lord too short to save? Or has his ear become heavy so as not to hear?' (Isa 59:1). But your sins divide among yourselves and between God. If God knows sins to separate men, nothing would be more grasping than that which, even by the truthful voice of Paul, the herald of truth, is called idolatry and is the root and mother of all evils.

For where did those who were once of the Christian party and partakers of the mysteries get drawn toward the worship of demons? Was it not by a love of possessing much and becoming masters of others' things? Having received promises from the atheists and the ungodly, either of a royal life or of wealth from the royal treasuries, they quickly changed their religion like a garment. And the memory and hearing of the former days of our life saved and taught.

But there is that which even our own life has delivered to trial. For when that king, having cast off the mask of the Christian continuously, and having stripped the comic drama which he had played for a long time, himself shamelessly offered sacrifices to demons and for those wishing to do this, he set many fees before them, how many, having left the church, ran to the altars? And how many, having accepted the bait of offices, followed after him with the hook of transgression? And accusers go about the cities, hated; being pointed out, traitors...

These men are Christ's for a little silver; they are outcasts from the Christian discourse, just as Judas was among the apostles. They are known by the sign of the runaway, like horses from their stalls, having been drawn only into the most difficult of all sins and having immediately followed the initiator of unholy and impure impiety.

Thus then, according to the apostle, greed and idolatry occur and are the root of all evils, having produced unsearchable wickedness from themselves (1 Timothy 6:10). For just as those searching for gold from the depths of the earth say that gold lies hidden safely in the earth at its beginning and its sovereign generation, but from there it flows out like certain veins here and there for a long distance and extends in many directions, like the roots of trees that pass through the soil, so also here I find many natures bound together by a single root, by greed.

And indeed, the word found no difficulty in using the example of gold for greed. From this I see the man daring to strike the head of the mother who gave birth, feeling no shame for either the closeness or the paternal dignity, but being weighed down by the desire for a longer life for the old man. For seeing everything abundant in the house and not having authority over what is seen, but desiring to be master of them and of the property, he is constricted by paternal authority.

And first he keeps silent and holds the disease in the depths; but with time, the desire increasing and the soul having been filled, he bursts forth with wickedness without restraint, like water through pipes. And so it is incomprehensible to the elder, only not...
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: The Fruits of Covetousness
english: Accompanying him to the tombs, walking healthily.

If he mounts the horse in a hurry, he is filled with pride; if he obtains more abundant food, he grumbles; if he wakes the servants early for their services, he is vexed by their waking and by the strength of the old man. But if he is given something of his treasures or if a servant is released from service, then and only then does he become a source of idle talk and wandering, exceeding the bounds of life and the things of others, a sword of the stranger, and he is provoked by hearing all blasphemy, asking why he did not die quickly.

Yours is this, O filthy greed, the fruit; from you the child becomes an enemy to the one who begot him, taking the stings. You fill the earth with robbers and murderers, submerge the sea, the cities with uproar, the courts with false witnesses, informers, traitors, accomplices, and judges who rule there wherever you drag them down.

Greed, the mother of inequality, pitiless, misanthropic, most wretched. Because of this, the life of man is full of irregularity; some, from the abundance of their possessions, sail upon the surplus as if it were an insatiable food, while others are pressed by hunger and want.

Some lie down under golden roofs and inhabit houses like small cities, adorned with baths, varied houses, and porticoes serving for a very long time and with every kind of luxury; others do not seem to have a roof, but when they cannot live in the open air, they flee to the furnaces of the baths or encounter bad innkeepers, and like pigs they root in the dung, devising for themselves the necessary warmth.

And the human being, the animal that is alike, has such a difference in diet compared to the kind that is alike; no one else has this disorder and this irregularity being introduced by greed. One is unseemly with his meals being meager, and another, to have his walls clothed in countless purple slabs, dresses them. The poor man lacks bread upon a wooden table, and the one enjoying luxury is entertained by the luster of the material, having spread a silver table wide. And how much more just was it for one to be satisfied with eating by another luxury, while the value of the table is the luxury of the destitute?

Another, old and unable to walk or limping due to some infirmity, does not possess a donkey, a necessary vehicle for his need; and another, because of a multitude of herds, does not know his horses. One is in want of oil to light a lamp; and another is rich with single lamps. One is thrown upon the ground, and the one who is wretchedly rich is surrounded by the world of the bed, having a silver sphere and chains instead of sheets.

These are the results of insatiable greed. For if it had not introduced inequality into life, these extremes and commonnesses would not have been, nor would the various misfortunes make our life unpleasantly tearful.
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: The Root of Conflict and Divine Providence
english: From this, men have destroyed natural friendship toward one another; they sharpen iron, form battle lines, and like wild beasts, they seize one another with great ferocity.

How could anyone even explain what follows this? Walls are besieged by engines, cities are plundered, women are led away, and children are enslaved; the earth is cut and plowed, and trees are fought over as if they were humans who had done wrong; and the slaughter of those in their prime is great, and the streams of blood flow from the wretched bodies; and the wealth of the defeated is the prize of the victors.

Upon these things are the wails of bereavement, the tears of orphans, and the lamenting of father and child together, and of liberty. The former master of great wealth now begs for a morsel of bread, stretching out his right hand; and he who once had many slaves, weaving fabrics and filling houses with clothing, now wears a rag and serves, carrying water out of necessity and unhitching the horse's pole and performing shameful services; and ten thousand other evils, which it is impossible to take in at once.

The beginning, cause, and root of all these things is the desire for more, the unjust love of the property of others. If anyone had cut off this passion of men, he would not have prevented peace from being lived deeply, nor wars and disturbances from fleeing from men, but all would have returned to natural affection and friendship.

For this reason also our Lord carefully allows this disease to pass by, sometimes forbidding: 'You cannot serve God and mammon' (Matt 6:24); sometimes rejecting that wretched rich man, who was about to die soon and was setting before himself the long-lasting enjoyment of luxury as a model; and elsewhere teaching that the perfect man is he who, having given away all that he has to those in need, will go his own way toward virtuous philosophy, the mother and companion of all things.

But I think I hear, even while being silent, such things being said to the teachers by those accustomed to them: 'And how shall we manage life if the possession of money is neglected? How shall we suffice for our needs? How shall a debt be settled? And how shall a loan be given to the one seeking, if we are all destitute because of your advice?' Unbelieving is the word, senseless is the voice, not knowing that we have God as Master, the steward of life, who provides for the living being from himself the useful things and the necessary supplies of food and the need of clothing.

For the providence of God regarding the things of His own is all-encompassing; and He has never withheld calamity from one who prospers in faith. And bringing forward one of the divine sayings as a sufficient testimony for what is at hand, I think, I shall provide a witness. In the history of the Kingdoms...

title: The Widow and Elisha
english: A certain woman is written about, a widow, being greatly weighed down by the misfortune of loneliness. A money-loving and misanthropic creditor was besieging her, taking away her sons, whom the mother had as her only ones instead of all. And when the matter stood for her in helplessness and no one having gold showed mercy, she came to the one possessing philanthropy and faith.

And this Elisha was the prophet, a man of the earthly substances being generous and abounding in the incorporeal possession; a philosopher from plowmen, unhoused, without support, living alone; having inherited recently, and having received the inheritance a widow's jar and an invisible blessing descending from the fiery chariot. He did not by any means send the entreaty unworked, nor did he reject the help because the sought-after thing was not present, nor did he say any base or faithless words, like one of the many: 'And from where to me is silver, so as to dissolve the debt?'

Just as an excellent physician and pharmacist, when not present, found the cure for the disease from extraordinary thoughts, so he says, 'What to you, O woman, upon the house? Remember if there is even a little inside.' For no one is so poor as to be suddenly the master of nothing. And as he said, that it is a jar and a little remnant of oil in it, 'Prepare for me,' he said, 'a multitude of vessels.' And she hurried, and he through it filled them, and to the creditor the debt was dissolved; and the woman departed from helplessness finding a way.

For the very little oil, which was to be with her, she said to the prophet, filled from the extraordinary and all the prepared amphorae; and then the flow stood, when there was no longer a vessel to receive; and to the need the grace was measured. Truly that was oil, which the plant did not bear, but the mercies of God flourished.

Acquire this knowledge, if you are able, kings, rulers, the wealthy, from the sun setting until it rises twice. You, the wise of the worldly wisdom, acquire the gift of the prophet from the plowmen, which was inexhaustible to the one receiving it. For the possessions of your zeal have myriad dangers lying in wait: robbers breaking through walls, tyrants snatching, and informers attacking, the sea sinking, and the earth being cracked by chasms.

Let there therefore be hope and a storehouse for men, the right hand of God, which led the people of Egypt out and in a desert land provided the abundance of good things; which led the Ambakum to Daniel, and saved Ishmael having been cast off from the mother's embrace, and sufficed to each generation, and lastly multiplied five barley loaves as if infinite agriculture, so that one loaf might fill the stomach of a thousand starving men and be enough for the basket of the remnants. To our God be the glory unto the ages of ages. Amen.
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: The False Celebration
english: The same Asterius's categorical discourse on the feast of the Kalends.

Two feasts have come together at once upon the yesterday and the present day, not in harmony or brotherhood, but on the contrary, holding enmity and opposition toward one another. For one is of the external gathering, bringing together much silver for Mammon and drawing in other trades, both in the marketplace and more freely; but the other is of holy and true worship, training the virtue of the relationship toward God and of a purified life.

Since many, preferring the luxury and idleness of vanity, have been left away from the assembly according to the church, come, let us drive away by word the foolish and harmful pleasure, just as one drives away a little madness in laughing and playing at death.

At the right time, let us imitate Solomon in the handling of the word. For he, advising the youths to keep themselves safely from the snares of immorality (Proverbs 7), so that his own exhortation might work as active and effective, personifies immorality as a woman condemned; and thus, by exposing all her wickedness, he decides the worth of hatred for those being enticed.
Therefore, I also, having shown the vanity of the human feast by word, will attempt to turn away the lovers of that fallen pursuit.

This custom and law is, therefore, a feast of the people; first, it is manifest that the purpose of the festival is to be a common joy for all, and not for one part to enjoy while the remainder spends the rest in grief and depression. For this is more like a war than a feast, since it is necessary for those who prevailed to parade in victory, and for those who were defeated to weep over their misfortune.
Regarding these days, first, it is unclear upon what the festival is celebrated. For myths...

Many things are said, which contradict one another; but nothing is true. Furthermore, I see only a few rejoicing; but the many are dejected, even if their sorrow is shaded by a decent appearance; and everything is full of noise and trouble, and the crowd is vainly pushed toward itself.

It is a remembrance and a joy of the year. What kind of joy, man? First, when I perceive the form of the meeting, that is, how suspicious and not friendly it is! The address proceeds with a dull and thin voice; then follows a kiss as a prelude to the bribe, and the mouth loves, but the coin is loved; the form of a disposition and the work of greed. But where pure friendship and guileless, unmercenary and sincere intentions exist.

Indeed, much is carried about everywhere and the gold is given, but a just and decent pretext for the bribe neither exists nor is spoken of. It is not a marriage, so that someone might call the bridegroom's zeal a wedding. I do not call the expense almsgiving; for no poor man is released from misfortune. No one would call what is happening a contract; for the crowd does not stir anything up among themselves. And to call it a gift is not even as far as being just, where necessity is joined to the giving.

What then shall we call, either the feast or the things spent in it? I myself do not find a name. But you, who have bitten through the crust around it, give a reason, as we are of the true and God-ordained festivals. We celebrate a birthday, because God showed us the theophanies in the flesh at this time. We lead a panegyric of lights, because through the forgiveness of sins we are led from a kind of dark prison of the former life toward the luminous and unconstrained.
We are made beautiful again and, rejoicing, we process on the day of the resurrection; for incorruption shows us a relocation toward the better. Thus these...

title: The Perils of Festive Debt
english: We celebrate in this way the appointed days; and for every human matter, talk is considered the leader; but where the cause and the goal are absent, this is mere chatter and vanity.

O, the absurdity! All those who have received wander about, hoping from one another. Those who receive are grieved, and those who have received do not hold on. For the gift passes to others, and the one receiving from the responsible party gives to the greater one. The gold of this day is unstable, like the ball of those playing, being sharply passed by me to the other.

And it is a new manner of gift-bearing and of service, having the contribution as a necessity. For the greater and more glorious one is shamed, the lesser one asks, and all move by steps upon the bosoms of the superior ones. And what happens during the rushing of the waters, this is now to be seen.

For there, a thin stream having flowed out mixes its currents with the one with it and the greater; and that one is covered again by the one more flooding, and many even thinner streams being gathered together become an addition to a neighboring river; this one again [passes] to another of the greater, and another to another, until the last one establishes the water by depth and breadth like the sea.

This feast is pseudonymous, full of extortion; for both the procession and the inner stay were not undisturbed. For the actors and the wonder-workers of the orchestra, having divided themselves into ranks and systems, wander through each house; and indeed they speak well and applaud, but they remain more conveniently at the gates of the practitioners, until the one inside is [cut off].

Silver, being besieged, goes before what it has and what it does not have. Approaching the doors in exchange, they receive one another, and until a late night there is no respite from evil, but one outcry takes hold of another, and one calamity of another.

This is the best feast and becomes the cause of loans for men, and of their offspring; a starting point of poverty, the beginning of misfortunes. If anyone, because of the unreliability of his substance, cannot even find a lender, he is dragged away like one failing to pay royal taxes, weeps like one being taken captive, is consumed like one who has fallen to a robber, is guarded, and is flogged.

If there is even a little in the house for the sustenance of a wife and struggling children, this is sent ahead; but those starving sit amidst the crowd during the bright feast. It is a new law of bad habit, to celebrate boredom and to call a general assembly of men's destitution.

This day teaches even small children to be grasping and simple-minded lovers of silver, and prepares them to plunder from house to house and to bring new gifts, while being bound by silver. But the giving of the double is a repayment, and from here the dishonest and the unrestrained begin to impress those with simple minds among the young.

And what does this day prepare for the holy and best farmers! It works for them a city that is fleeing and unapproachable; and more so are they paying it back than hares [pay back] the nets. For those found are flogged, are reproached, lose what is in their hands, are fought against in peace, are insulted, and are mocked by words and deeds.
